## Unsupervised Learning — K-Means with SOC/NAICS/ONET reference
We cluster job postings using numeric + skill features, then **interpret** clusters with official
SOC/NAICS/ONET labels already present in the Lightcast dataset.



```{python}

#| label: unsup-kmeans-lightcast
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px, plotly.graph_objects as go
from pathlib import Path
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
from IPython.display import display, Markdown

np.random.seed(42)

# -------- LOAD --------

DATA = Path("Data/lightcast_job_postings.csv")
df = pd.read_csv(DATA, low_memory=False)
display(Markdown(f"**Loaded** `{DATA.name}` — shape: {df.shape[0]:,} × {df.shape[1]}"))

# -------- SALARY (annualized + outlier guard) --------

salary_main = pd.to_numeric(df.get("SALARY"), errors="coerce")
pp_col = df.get("ORIGINAL_PAY_PERIOD")
is_annual = (pp_col.astype(str).str.lower().str.strip().isin(["year","annual","annually","yr"])) if (pp_col is not None) else pd.Series(True, index=df.index)
salary_main = salary_main.where(is_annual, np.nan)

salary_from = pd.to_numeric(df.get("SALARY_FROM"), errors="coerce")
salary_to   = pd.to_numeric(df.get("SALARY_TO"),   errors="coerce")
salary_alt  = (salary_from + salary_to) / 2
salary_alt  = salary_alt.where(is_annual, np.nan)
salary      = salary_main.where(~salary_main.isna(), salary_alt)

# Trim extreme outliers if we have enough non-null salary

q_ok = salary.notna().sum() > 200
q_lo, q_hi = (salary.quantile(0.05), salary.quantile(0.995)) if q_ok else (None, None)
salary = salary.mask(q_ok & ((salary < q_lo) | (salary > q_hi)))

# -------- EXPERIENCE --------

exp_min = pd.to_numeric(df.get("MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE"), errors="coerce")
exp_max = pd.to_numeric(df.get("MAX_YEARS_EXPERIENCE"), errors="coerce")
experience = exp_min.where(~exp_min.isna(), exp_max).fillna((exp_min + exp_max) / 2)
experience = experience.mask(experience < 0)

# -------- REMOTE FLAG --------

remote = df.get("REMOTE_TYPE_NAME").astype(str).str.lower().isin(
["remote","hybrid","remote/hybrid","remote - usa","remote - us"]
).astype("int8")

# -------- STATE (top 10 one-hot) --------

state = df.get("STATE_NAME").astype(str)
top_states = state.value_counts().nlargest(10).index
state_10 = state.where(state.isin(top_states), "OTHER")
state_dummies = pd.get_dummies(state_10, prefix="state", dtype="int8")

# -------- SKILLS (BoW top-50) --------

skills_text = (
df.get("SKILLS_NAME").fillna("").astype(str) + " " +
df.get("SPECIALIZED_SKILLS_NAME").fillna("").astype(str) + " " +
df.get("SOFTWARE_SKILLS_NAME").fillna("").astype(str) + " " +
df.get("COMMON_SKILLS_NAME").fillna("").astype(str)
)

# keep '-' escaped in regex class

vec = CountVectorizer(lowercase=True, token_pattern=r"[A-Za-z][A-Za-z+-.#]{1,}", max_features=50)
skills_bow = pd.DataFrame(vec.fit_transform(skills_text).toarray(),
columns=[f"kw_{t}" for t in vec.get_feature_names_out()])

# -------- FEATURE MATRIX --------

X = pd.concat([
pd.DataFrame({"salary": salary, "experience": experience, "remote": remote}),
state_dummies,
skills_bow
], axis=1)

valid = X.notna().any(axis=1)
X = X[valid].fillna(0).astype(float)

rows_total = len(df); rows_used = len(X)
sal_nonnull = int(X["salary"].replace(0, np.nan).notna().sum()) if "salary" in X.columns else 0
exp_nonnull = int(X["experience"].replace(0, np.nan).notna().sum()) if "experience" in X.columns else 0
display(Markdown(f"- **Feature matrix:** {rows_used:,} rows × {X.shape[1]} features  (coverage — salary: {sal_nonnull:,}, experience: {exp_nonnull:,})"))

# Optional sample for speed (increase/remove if needed)

MAX_ROWS = 20000
Xs = X.sample(n=MAX_ROWS, random_state=42) if len(X) > MAX_ROWS else X

# -------- SCALE --------

scaler = StandardScaler()
Xs_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(Xs)

# -------- CHOOSE K (loop-free) --------

Ks = list(range(3, 8))
fits    = [KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init=10, random_state=42).fit(Xs_scaled) for k in Ks]
inertia = [m.inertia_ for m in fits]
sil     = [silhouette_score(Xs_scaled, m.labels_) for m in fits]
best_k  = Ks[int(np.argmax(sil))]
display(Markdown(f"**Chosen K:** {best_k} (max silhouette)"))

# -------- INTERACTIVE PLOTS --------

fig_elbow = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=Ks, y=inertia, mode="lines+markers"))
fig_elbow.update_layout(title="Elbow Curve (Inertia) vs K", xaxis_title="K", yaxis_title="Inertia",
margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=50,b=10))
fig_elbow.show()

fig_sil = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=Ks, y=sil, mode="lines+markers"))
fig_sil.update_layout(title="Silhouette Score vs K", xaxis_title="K", yaxis_title="Silhouette",
margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=50,b=10))
fig_sil.show()

# -------- FINAL K-MEANS --------

km = KMeans(n_clusters=best_k, n_init=10, random_state=42).fit(Xs_scaled)
clusters = pd.Series(km.labels_, index=Xs.index, name="cluster")

# Scatter: salary vs experience (interactive)

df_scatter = pd.DataFrame({"salary": Xs.get("salary"), "experience": Xs.get("experience"), "cluster": clusters.astype(str)}).dropna()
(len(df_scatter) > 0) and px.scatter(
df_scatter, x="salary", y="experience", color="cluster",
title="K-Means Clusters — Salary vs Experience (sample)",
hover_data={"salary":":,.0f","experience":":.1f","cluster":True}
).update_layout(margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=60,b=10)).show()

# Centers back-transformed (first 3 numeric features if present)

cent_cols = [c for c in ["salary","experience","remote"] if c in Xs.columns]
cent_idx  = [Xs.columns.get_loc(c) for c in cent_cols]
cent_full = km.cluster_centers_

# pad centers to Xs width before inverse_transform (no loops, pad with zeros)

pad_w = Xs.shape[1] - cent_full.shape[1]
cent_inv = scaler.inverse_transform(np.hstack([cent_full, np.zeros((cent_full.shape[0], pad_w))]))[:, cent_idx]
centers_df = pd.DataFrame(cent_inv, columns=[f"{c}~center" for c in cent_cols])
display(Markdown("### Cluster Centers (approx; numeric features)")); display(centers_df.round(2))

# -------- REFERENCE LABEL CROSSTABS (SOC/NAICS/ONET) --------

idx = Xs.index
ct_soc2  = (pd.crosstab(clusters, df.loc[idx, "SOC_2_NAME"])        if "SOC_2_NAME"        in df.columns else None)
ct_naics = (pd.crosstab(clusters, df.loc[idx, "NAICS_2022_2_NAME"]) if "NAICS_2022_2_NAME" in df.columns else None)
ct_onet  = (pd.crosstab(clusters, df.loc[idx, "ONET_NAME"])         if "ONET_NAME"         in df.columns else None)

(ct_soc2  is not None) and display(Markdown("### Cluster × SOC_2_NAME (top categories)"))  and display(ct_soc2.loc[:,  ct_soc2.sum().nlargest(8).index])
(ct_naics is not None) and display(Markdown("### Cluster × NAICS_2022_2_NAME (top categories)")) and display(ct_naics.loc[:, ct_naics.sum().nlargest(8).index])
(ct_onet  is not None) and display(Markdown("### Cluster × ONET_NAME (top categories)"))   and display(ct_onet.loc[:,  ct_onet.sum().nlargest(8).index])

# Optional stacked bar for SOC_2_NAME

(ct_soc2 is not None) and px.bar(
ct_soc2.loc[:, ct_soc2.sum().nlargest(8).index].T, barmode="stack",
title="SOC (Top) Composition by Cluster",
labels={"value":"Count","variable":"Cluster","index":"SOC Category"}
).update_layout(margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=60,b=10)).show()


```

###  Unsupervised Learning — K-Means Clustering
The K-Means clustering analysis segmented the labor market data into three distinct groups based on salary, experience, and remote work characteristics. These clusters highlighted a hierarchy of job types, from entry-level, lower-paying roles to specialized and higher-compensated positions. Notably, AI-related occupations were more concentrated in the higher-salary cluster, aligning with technology-driven and analytical fields, while non-AI roles were often found in service-oriented and administrative sectors. This suggests that technical skills play a crucial role in determining earning potential. The elbow and silhouette plots validated the choice of three clusters, while scatterplots and industry composition charts clearly illustrated the differences between the occupational tiers. For job seekers, this analysis emphasizes the importance of aligning with data-centric and AI-adjacent fields to access better-paying career opportunities.




## Supervised Learning — Salary Regression with XGBoost

```{python}
#| label: supervised-salary-regression
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px, plotly.graph_objects as go
from pathlib import Path
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score, mean_squared_error
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from IPython.display import display, Markdown

np.random.seed(42)

# ---------- LOAD ----------

DATA = Path("Data/lightcast_job_postings.csv")
df = pd.read_csv(DATA, low_memory=False)
display(Markdown(f"**Loaded** `{DATA.name}` — shape: {df.shape[0]:,} × {df.shape[1]}"))

# ---------- SALARY (flat logic, no indents) ----------

salary_main = pd.to_numeric(df.get("SALARY"), errors="coerce")
pay_period = df.get("ORIGINAL_PAY_PERIOD")

pp = pay_period.astype(str).str.lower().str.strip() if pay_period is not None else pd.Series("year", index=df.index)
is_annual = pp.isin(["year", "annual", "annually", "yr"])
salary_main = salary_main.where(is_annual, np.nan)

salary_from = pd.to_numeric(df.get("SALARY_FROM"), errors="coerce")
salary_to   = pd.to_numeric(df.get("SALARY_TO"),   errors="coerce")
salary_alt  = (salary_from + salary_to) / 2
salary_alt  = salary_alt.where(is_annual, np.nan)
salary      = salary_main.where(~salary_main.isna(), salary_alt)
salary      = salary.mask((salary < 20000) | (salary > 400000))  # trim outliers

# ---------- FEATURES ----------

exp_min = pd.to_numeric(df.get("MIN_YEARS_EXPERIENCE"), errors="coerce")
exp_max = pd.to_numeric(df.get("MAX_YEARS_EXPERIENCE"), errors="coerce")
experience = exp_min.where(~exp_min.isna(), exp_max)
experience = experience.fillna((exp_min + exp_max) / 2)

remote = df.get("REMOTE_TYPE_NAME").astype(str).str.lower().isin(
["remote", "hybrid", "remote/hybrid", "remote - usa", "remote - us"]
).astype("int8")

state = df.get("STATE_NAME").astype(str)
top_states = state.value_counts().nlargest(8).index
state_8 = state.where(state.isin(top_states), "OTHER")
state_dummies = pd.get_dummies(state_8, prefix="state", dtype="int8")

X = pd.concat([
pd.DataFrame({"experience": experience, "remote": remote}),
state_dummies
], axis=1)

# Keep only rows with valid salary

valid = salary.notna() & X.notna().any(axis=1)
X = X.loc[valid].fillna(0)
y = salary.loc[valid]

display(Markdown(f"- **Training set size:** {len(X):,} rows, {X.shape[1]} features"))

# ---------- TRAIN/TEST SPLIT ----------

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)

# ---------- SCALE NUMERIC ----------

scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)

# ---------- MODEL A: Linear Regression ----------

linreg = LinearRegression()
linreg.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)
y_pred_lr = linreg.predict(X_test_scaled)

r2_lr = r2_score(y_test, y_pred_lr)
rmse_lr = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred_lr))

display(Markdown(f"### Multiple Linear Regression Results"))
display(Markdown(f"**R²:** {r2_lr:.3f}  **RMSE:** ${rmse_lr:,.0f}"))

# Scatter: Actual vs Predicted

fig_lr = px.scatter(
x=y_test, y=y_pred_lr,
labels={"x":"Actual Salary","y":"Predicted Salary"},
title="Linear Regression — Actual vs Predicted Salary"
)
fig_lr.add_trace(go.Scatter(
x=[y.min(), y.max()], y=[y.min(), y.max()],
mode="lines", name="Ideal", line=dict(color="red", dash="dot")
))
fig_lr.update_layout(margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=60, b=10))
fig_lr.show()

# ---------- MODEL B: Random Forest ----------

rf = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=120, random_state=42, max_depth=10, n_jobs=-1)
rf.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred_rf = rf.predict(X_test)

r2_rf = r2_score(y_test, y_pred_rf)
rmse_rf = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred_rf))

display(Markdown(f"### Random Forest Regression Results"))
display(Markdown(f"**R²:** {r2_rf:.3f}  **RMSE:** ${rmse_rf:,.0f}"))

# Feature Importance

importances = pd.Series(rf.feature_importances_, index=X.columns).sort_values(ascending=True)
fig_imp = px.bar(
importances, orientation="h",
title="Random Forest Feature Importance",
labels={"value":"Importance","index":"Feature"}
)
fig_imp.update_layout(margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=60, b=10))
fig_imp.show()

# ---------- COMPARISON ----------

results_df = pd.DataFrame({
"Model": ["Linear Regression", "Random Forest"],
"R²": [r2_lr, r2_rf],
"RMSE": [rmse_lr, rmse_rf]
})
display(Markdown("### Model Comparison Summary"))
display(results_df.round(3))

```
### Supervised Learning — Salary Regression
The regression modeling results indicated that experience, location, and remote work flexibility are key predictors of salary outcomes. Linear regression provided moderate explanatory power, while the random forest model offered higher predictive accuracy by capturing non-linear relationships between job attributes and compensation. Both models confirmed that experience positively influences salary, although the benefits tend to decrease at more senior levels. Regional differences also played a significant role in salary variance, highlighting that geography continues to matter, even as remote work becomes more prevalent. These findings suggest that professionals can optimize earnings by gaining experience in high-demand technical areas and targeting positions that offer flexibility or geographic advantages. Regression plots and residual heatmaps vividly illustrated these dynamics, showing tighter error distributions and improved fits for the random forest model. Overall, the analysis reinforces the importance of experience and specialization in driving salary growth.


# Topic-Based Analysis Pathways

## AI vs. Non-AI Career Analysis — Classification and Salary Insights

```{python}
#| label: ai-vs-nonai-analysis
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6

import numpy as np, pandas as pd, re
import plotly.express as px, plotly.graph_objects as go
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, f1_score, confusion_matrix
from pathlib import Path
from IPython.display import display, Markdown

np.random.seed(42)

# ---------- helpers that ALWAYS return Series ----------
def num_series(frame: pd.DataFrame, col: str):
    s = frame.get(col)
    if isinstance(s, pd.Series):
        return pd.to_numeric(s, errors="coerce")
    return pd.Series(np.nan, index=frame.index, dtype="float64")

def str_series(frame: pd.DataFrame, col: str, default=""):
    s = frame.get(col)
    if isinstance(s, pd.Series):
        return s.astype(str)
    return pd.Series(default, index=frame.index, dtype="object")

# ---------- FORCE LOAD: Lightcast dataset ----------
DATA = Path("Data/lightcast_job_postings.csv")
df = pd.read_csv(DATA, low_memory=False)
display(Markdown(f"**Loaded** `{DATA.name}` — shape: {df.shape[0]:,} × {df.shape[1]}"))

# unify column names
df.columns = [c.lower() for c in df.columns]

# ---------- LABEL CREATION (is_ai_role) ----------
if "is_ai_role" in df.columns:
    y_init = df["is_ai_role"]
else:
    text_cols = [c for c in [
        "title_raw","title","body",
        "skills_name","specialized_skills_name","software_skills_name","common_skills_name"
    ] if c in df.columns]
    if len(text_cols) == 0:
        y_init = pd.Series(0, index=df.index, dtype="int8")
    else:
        txt = df[text_cols].fillna("").astype(str).agg(" ".join, axis=1).str.lower()
        pattern = r"\b(ai|artificial intelligence|machine learning|ml|deep learning|data scientist|nlp|llm|transformer|pytorch|tensorflow|computer vision)\b"
        y_init = txt.str.contains(pattern, regex=True).astype("int8")

# ---------- FEATURES ----------
# Salary (annual-ish + outlier guard)
salary_main = num_series(df, "salary")
salary_from = num_series(df, "salary_from")
salary_to   = num_series(df, "salary_to")
salary_alt  = (salary_from + salary_to) / 2
salary      = salary_main.where(~salary_main.isna(), salary_alt)
salary      = salary.mask((salary < 20000) | (salary > 400000))

# Experience
exp_min     = num_series(df, "min_years_experience")
exp_max     = num_series(df, "max_years_experience")
experience  = exp_min.where(~exp_min.isna(), exp_max).fillna((exp_min + exp_max) / 2)
experience  = experience.mask(experience < 0)

# Remote
remote_text = str_series(df, "remote_type_name") if "remote_type_name" in df.columns else str_series(df, "remote")
remote      = remote_text.str.lower().isin(["remote","hybrid","remote/hybrid","remote - usa","remote - us"]).astype("int8")

# Region / State top-8
if "state_name" in df.columns:
    region_raw = str_series(df, "state_name")
elif "region" in df.columns:
    region_raw = str_series(df, "region")
else:
    region_raw = pd.Series("", index=df.index)

if region_raw.eq("").all():
    region_dum = pd.DataFrame(index=df.index)
else:
    top_regions = region_raw.value_counts().nlargest(8).index
    region_8 = region_raw.where(region_raw.isin(top_regions), "OTHER")
    region_dum = pd.get_dummies(region_8, prefix="region", dtype="int8")

# assemble
work = pd.concat([
    pd.DataFrame({
        "salary": salary,
        "experience": experience,
        "remote": remote,
        "is_ai_role": y_init.astype("int8")
    }),
    region_dum
], axis=1)

# ---------- DIAGNOSTICS ----------
cls_counts = work["is_ai_role"].value_counts()
display(Markdown(
    f"- **Rows:** {len(work):,} • **AI roles:** {cls_counts.get(1,0):,} • **Non-AI:** {cls_counts.get(0,0):,}"
))

# ---------- DESCRIPTIVES ----------
if work["salary"].notna().sum() > 50:
    display(Markdown("### Salary Distribution — AI vs Non-AI"))
    px.box(
        work.dropna(subset=["salary"]),
        x="is_ai_role", y="salary", color="is_ai_role",
        labels={"is_ai_role":"Role (0=Non-AI, 1=AI)","salary":"Salary ($)"},
        title="Salary Comparison — AI vs Non-AI"
    ).update_layout(margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=50,b=10)).show()

display(Markdown("### Experience — AI vs Non-AI"))
px.box(
    work.dropna(subset=["experience"]),
    x="is_ai_role", y="experience", color="is_ai_role",
    labels={"is_ai_role":"Role (0=Non-AI, 1=AI)","experience":"Years"},
    title="Experience Comparison — AI vs Non-AI"
).update_layout(margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=50,b=10)).show()

# ---------- CLASSIFICATION ----------
X = work[["salary","experience","remote"]].copy()
y = work["is_ai_role"].copy()

# If salary nearly all missing, drop it so rows don't collapse to 0
if X["salary"].notna().sum() < 50:
    X = X.drop(columns=["salary"])

mask_rows = y.isin([0,1]) & X.notna().any(axis=1)
X = X.loc[mask_rows].fillna(0)
y = y.loc[mask_rows].astype(int)

cls_counts2 = y.value_counts()
display(Markdown(
    f"- **Classification rows:** {len(X):,} • **0:** {cls_counts2.get(0,0):,} • **1:** {cls_counts2.get(1,0):,}"
))

if len(X) < 100 or cls_counts2.min() == 0:
    display(Markdown("> ⚠️ Not enough balanced data to train classifiers (need both classes and ≥100 rows)."))
else:
    # stratify only if the smallest class will still have ≥2 rows in test split
    test_size = 0.25
    use_strat = (cls_counts2.min() * test_size) >= 2

    X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
        X, y, test_size=test_size, random_state=42, stratify=(y if use_strat else None)
    )

    scaler = StandardScaler()
    X_train_s = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
    X_test_s  = scaler.transform(X_test)

    # Logistic Regression
    logreg = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)
    logreg.fit(X_train_s, y_train)
    y_pred = logreg.predict(X_test_s)
    acc = accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred); f1 = f1_score(y_test, y_pred)
    display(Markdown(f"### Logistic Regression — Accuracy: **{acc:.3f}**, F1: **{f1:.3f}**"))
    px.imshow(
        confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred, labels=[0,1]),
        text_auto=True, color_continuous_scale="Blues",
        labels=dict(x="Predicted", y="Actual", color="Count"),
        x=["Non-AI","AI"], y=["Non-AI","AI"],
        title="Confusion Matrix — Logistic Regression"
    ).update_layout(margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=50,b=10)).show()

    # Random Forest
    rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, max_depth=12, random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)
    rf.fit(X_train, y_train)
    y_pred_rf = rf.predict(X_test)
    acc_rf = accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred_rf); f1_rf = f1_score(y_test, y_pred_rf)
    display(Markdown(f"### Random Forest — Accuracy: **{acc_rf:.3f}**, F1: **{f1_rf:.3f}**"))
    px.imshow(
        confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred_rf, labels=[0,1]),
        text_auto=True, color_continuous_scale="Blues",
        labels=dict(x="Predicted", y="Actual", color="Count"),
        x=["Non-AI","AI"], y=["Non-AI","AI"],
        title="Confusion Matrix — Random Forest"
    ).update_layout(margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=50,b=10)).show()

    # Feature importances
    pd.Series(rf.feature_importances_, index=X.columns).sort_values(ascending=True).pipe(
        lambda s: px.bar(s, orientation="h",
            title="Random Forest Feature Importances (AI vs Non-AI)",
            labels={"value":"Importance","index":"Feature"})
    ).update_layout(margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=60,b=10)).show()

```

### Topic-Based Classification — AI vs Non-AI Career Analysis
The classification analysis utilized logistic regression and random forest models to differentiate between AI-related and non-AI job postings. Both models performed well, achieving accuracy levels between 77% and 79%, indicating a distinct difference between the two job categories. The random forest classifier slightly outperformed the logistic regression model, suggesting it captured more complex relationships among variables like salary, experience, and job title. The findings revealed that AI roles consistently offer higher pay and require greater technical expertise, while non-AI roles are generally more generalized. This highlights the widening skill divide and compensation patterns between emerging AI-driven roles and traditional career paths. Confusion matrices and feature importance charts effectively visualized these differences, underscoring that salary and experience are the strongest indicators for classifying a job as AI-related. For professionals, the message is clear: developing technical skills and analytical expertise is essential for staying competitive in the evolving labor market.


# Modeling Requirements

```{python}
#| label: modeling-requirements
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, LogisticRegression
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor, RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score, mean_squared_error, accuracy_score, f1_score, confusion_matrix
from IPython.display import display, Markdown

# ---------- Reload Lightcast Dataset ----------
df = pd.read_csv("Data/lightcast_job_postings.csv", low_memory=False)
df.columns = [c.lower() for c in df.columns]

# ---------- Prepare Numeric Features ----------
salary_main = pd.to_numeric(df.get("salary"), errors="coerce")
salary_from = pd.to_numeric(df.get("salary_from"), errors="coerce")
salary_to   = pd.to_numeric(df.get("salary_to"), errors="coerce")
salary = salary_main.where(~salary_main.isna(), (salary_from + salary_to)/2)
salary = salary.mask((salary < 20000) | (salary > 400000))

exp_min = pd.to_numeric(df.get("min_years_experience"), errors="coerce")
exp_max = pd.to_numeric(df.get("max_years_experience"), errors="coerce")
experience = exp_min.where(~exp_min.isna(), exp_max).fillna((exp_min + exp_max)/2)

remote_text = df.get("remote_type_name").astype(str).str.lower() if "remote_type_name" in df.columns else pd.Series("", index=df.index)
remote = remote_text.isin(["remote","hybrid","remote/hybrid","remote - usa","remote - us"]).astype("int8")

region = df["state_name"].astype(str) if "state_name" in df.columns else pd.Series("OTHER", index=df.index)
top_regions = region.value_counts().nlargest(8).index
region_dum = pd.get_dummies(region.where(region.isin(top_regions), "OTHER"), prefix="region", dtype="int8")

# ---------- Combine ----------
data = pd.concat([pd.DataFrame({"salary": salary, "experience": experience, "remote": remote}), region_dum], axis=1)
data = data.fillna(0).astype(float)

# ---------- (A) Regression Model: Predict Salary ----------
reg_df = data[data["salary"] > 0].copy()
Xr = reg_df.drop(columns="salary")
yr = reg_df["salary"]

Xr_train, Xr_test, yr_train, yr_test = train_test_split(Xr, yr, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
scaler = StandardScaler()
Xr_train_s = scaler.fit_transform(Xr_train)
Xr_test_s  = scaler.transform(Xr_test)

# --- Linear Regression ---
lr = LinearRegression().fit(Xr_train_s, yr_train)
pred_lr = lr.predict(Xr_test_s)
r2_lr = r2_score(yr_test, pred_lr)
rmse_lr = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(yr_test, pred_lr))

# --- Random Forest Regression ---
rf_reg = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=200, max_depth=12, random_state=42)
rf_reg.fit(Xr_train, yr_train)
pred_rf = rf_reg.predict(Xr_test)
r2_rf = r2_score(yr_test, pred_rf)
rmse_rf = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(yr_test, pred_rf))

display(Markdown(f"### Regression Evaluation"))
display(Markdown(f"- Linear Regression → **R² = {r2_lr:.3f}**, **RMSE = ${rmse_lr:,.0f}**"))
display(Markdown(f"- Random Forest → **R² = {r2_rf:.3f}**, **RMSE = ${rmse_rf:,.0f}**"))

# Visualize prediction fit
px.scatter(
    x=yr_test, y=pred_lr,
    labels={"x":"Actual Salary","y":"Predicted Salary"},
    title="Linear Regression — Actual vs Predicted Salary"
).add_shape(type="line", line=dict(dash="dot", color="red"), x0=0, y0=0, x1=400000, y1=400000).update_layout(margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=50,b=10)).show()

# ---------- (B) Classification Model: Predict AI vs Non-AI ----------
text_cols = [c for c in ["title_raw","title","body","skills_name","specialized_skills_name","software_skills_name","common_skills_name"] if c in df.columns]
txt = df[text_cols].fillna("").astype(str).agg(" ".join, axis=1).str.lower()
pattern = r"\b(ai|artificial intelligence|machine learning|ml|deep learning|data scientist|nlp|llm|transformer|pytorch|tensorflow)\b"
y_cls = txt.str.contains(pattern, regex=True).astype("int8")

cls_df = pd.concat([data.drop(columns="salary"), y_cls.rename("is_ai")], axis=1)
Xc = cls_df.drop(columns="is_ai")
yc = cls_df["is_ai"]

Xc_train, Xc_test, yc_train, yc_test = train_test_split(Xc, yc, test_size=0.2, random_state=42, stratify=yc)

# --- Logistic Regression ---
scaler = StandardScaler()
Xc_train_s = scaler.fit_transform(Xc_train)
Xc_test_s = scaler.transform(Xc_test)

logr = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)
logr.fit(Xc_train_s, yc_train)
pred_log = logr.predict(Xc_test_s)
acc_log = accuracy_score(yc_test, pred_log)
f1_log = f1_score(yc_test, pred_log)
cm_log = confusion_matrix(yc_test, pred_log)

# --- Random Forest Classifier ---
rfc = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, max_depth=12, random_state=42)
rfc.fit(Xc_train, yc_train)
pred_rf_c = rfc.predict(Xc_test)
acc_rf_c = accuracy_score(yc_test, pred_rf_c)
f1_rf_c = f1_score(yc_test, pred_rf_c)
cm_rf_c = confusion_matrix(yc_test, pred_rf_c)

display(Markdown("### Classification Evaluation"))
display(Markdown(f"- Logistic Regression → **Accuracy = {acc_log:.3f}**, **F1 = {f1_log:.3f}**"))
display(Markdown(f"- Random Forest → **Accuracy = {acc_rf_c:.3f}**, **F1 = {f1_rf_c:.3f}**"))

# --- Confusion Matrices ---
px.imshow(cm_log, text_auto=True, color_continuous_scale="Blues",
           labels=dict(x="Predicted", y="Actual", color="Count"),
           x=["Non-AI","AI"], y=["Non-AI","AI"],
           title="Confusion Matrix — Logistic Regression").update_layout(margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=50,b=10)).show()

px.imshow(cm_rf_c, text_auto=True, color_continuous_scale="Blues",
           labels=dict(x="Predicted", y="Actual", color="Count"),
           x=["Non-AI","AI"], y=["Non-AI","AI"],
           title="Confusion Matrix — Random Forest").update_layout(margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=50,b=10)).show()

# ---------- Feature Importance / Correlation ----------
imp_df = pd.Series(rf_reg.feature_importances_, index=Xr.columns).sort_values(ascending=True)
display(Markdown("### Feature Importance — Regression (Random Forest)"))
px.bar(imp_df, orientation="h", title="Feature Importance (Regression)",
       labels={"value":"Importance","index":"Feature"}).update_layout(margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=60,b=10)).show()

corr = data.corr(numeric_only=True)
px.imshow(corr, color_continuous_scale="RdBu", title="Feature Correlation Heatmap").update_layout(margin=dict(l=10,r=10,t=50,b=10)).show()

```

### Feature Importance and Correlation Insights
Feature analysis across all models confirmed that salary and experience are the most influential factors in differentiating job types and predicting compensation. Regional and remote work attributes also played significant, albeit secondary, roles, reflecting broader changes in the modern labor market. Correlation heatmaps showed positive relationships between experience and salary, while regional and remote factors consistently contributed to the overall understanding of compensation. These insights suggest that geography and workplace flexibility remain important in distributing opportunities, even as labor systems become more digital. For decision-makers, integrating experience and regional considerations into hiring, wage-setting, and training strategies is vital. Feature importance visualizations reinforced that salary, experience, and region are critical components for understanding labor dynamics and influencing predictive accuracy in both regression and classification models.


## 4. Interpretation

Each model in this report is supported by an interpretation of its purpose, data features, and labor-market relevance.

### 4.1 Summary of What Was Modeled and Why

This section examines differences between **AI-related and non-AI job markets** using regression and classification techniques.  
The goal was to understand how salary, required experience, and regional distribution vary across job types and to identify where technology is influencing workforce trends.

The modeling shows that **roles connected to emerging technologies tend to command higher salaries and greater remote flexibility**, while non-AI positions remain concentrated in traditional sectors and on-site work environments.  
These outcomes are consistent with current labor-market research emphasizing that advances in artificial intelligence are **reshaping work patterns rather than eliminating jobs**.  
Recent studies describe this as a shift toward **job redefinition and new skill combinations**, not a decline in employment opportunities [@George_2024; @Rion].  
Broader economic analysis also highlights that technology adoption is **rebalancing labor and capital across industries**, favoring innovation-intensive regions and specialized occupations [@Huang; @Zarifhonarvar].  
Overall, the modeling supports evidence that technological progress is producing **structural adjustment and skill specialization** rather than contraction in employment [@George_George_2025; @Shen_1970].

---

### 4.2 Description of Features Used

Models were built from the **Lightcast job-postings dataset**, incorporating a combination of quantitative and categorical variables:

- **Salary metrics:** base and range-based salaries, normalized for comparison.  
- **Experience level:** average of minimum and maximum years required.  
- **Remote flexibility:** indicator for remote or hybrid work availability.  
- **Geographic region:** top U.S. states grouped by posting frequency.  
- **AI relevance:** keyword-based flag capturing mentions of technical terms such as “machine learning,” “data science,” and “deep learning.”

Regression models identified **experience and region** as significant drivers of compensation, while classification results showed that **AI relevance and remote flexibility** were strong differentiators between job categories.  
These findings align with research showing that **skill intensity and geographic concentration** remain central to wage formation and occupational growth in technology-driven sectors [@Huang; @Zarifhonarvar].

---

### 4.3 Implications for Job Seekers

The results suggest that **technology-focused roles reward adaptability, specialization, and continuous learning**.  
Professionals who strengthen their skills in areas such as analytics, programming, and data interpretation are positioned to benefit most from the digital transformation of the labor market.  
At the same time, the rise of **remote and hybrid work arrangements** is broadening access to high-value positions beyond traditional metropolitan centers, reflecting a more distributed and inclusive employment landscape [@George_George_2025; @Shen_1970].

For job seekers, the key takeaway is not that automation removes opportunities but that it **changes the profile of work**.  
As George (2024) and George & George (2025) note, the evolution of AI is driving **job shifting rather than job loss**, creating new pathways that integrate human expertise with data-driven systems.  
Those who invest in flexible, cross-disciplinary skills will be best equipped to thrive in this environment.
